title: I made a card game entirely with AI. The hardest part was keeping art, rules and translations in sync
author: grejanin
selftext:
I built \*Treat Tussle\*, a free browser card game for 2–6 players. Everyone draws from the same deck. There are 20 different food characters across five factions, and each card gives you three abilities to choose from. I used generative AI for the art, code, writing, and Portuguese-to-English localization. The game runs on ordinary rules code, including when a bot takes a turn.



\*\*1. A balance patch can leave a perfectly readable card telling a lie.\*\* My card fronts are finished illustrations, right down to the rules text. When I changed an ability in code, the game played correctly while the old image still taught players the old rule. I now take the wording from the card definitions when revising a front. For the Christmas cards I tried a different approach that already works in the game: the illustration comes from an image file, and the game draws the ability text over it.



\*\*2. The hardest part of translating a card was the last line.\*\* For the English Halloween cards, I gave the image model the approved Portuguese front and the exact English strings for all three panels. One instruction mattered more than anything about style: "fit legible text by adjusting font size and line wrapping, never omit or shorten rules." On \*Pepper Dynamite\*, the third attack continues only if the previous opponent was eliminated. Lose that condition to save a line and you've just designed a much stronger card.



\*\*3. I had to name things before translating them.\*\* I wanted a player to remember a joke after seeing a card once. A literal translation rarely did that for me. I settled on \*Pepper Dynamite\* for the character, \*Hot Poke\* for its first ability, and \*Chiliarchy\* for its faction. I kept the approved names together so the card, the tutorial, and the next art prompt would all use the same joke.



\*\*4. The bots gave me a result I wouldn't have guessed.\*\* In an early balance pass I compared two batches of 5,000 simulated matches using the same seeds, table sizes, and bot profiles. I had capped the health change from two tea abilities at four points per player. It fixed the huge health swings. But with defensive bots, almost every match hit the 500-turn cutoff (only about one in a thousand finished earlier), both before and after the change. That helped me separate two questions: did the ability do what I intended, and did people enjoy how the match played? I used automated tests for interactions like shields, lethal damage, and turn direction, and closed testing with people for the experience of playing.



\*\*5. I judged the art at the size of a card in someone's hand.\*\* For the dough faction I used two approved fronts from other factions as visual references, so I had the proportions, lettering, and ability panels in front of me. My first Halloween pepper looked like a small character pasted into a big empty rectangle. The version I kept had a Halloween scene around the character, with the title and all three ability panels still in their familiar places. Enlarged, you can enjoy the costume. In your hand, you can still tell which card you drew.



I used ChatGPT for writing and localization, OpenAI's image generation tool for card art and edits, and Codex for implementation and tests. The game is playable in \[English and Brazilian Portuguese on itch.io\](https://grejanin.itch.io/treat-tussle).



For anyone making cards with generated art: which parts of the card do you keep as images, and which do you render from game data? I'd especially like to hear how you kept the lettering looking like it belonged on the card after moving it out of the illustration.
